svg.text: The rights of administration — and the three nobody teaches
The five you already know
Right PATIENT — two identifiers
Right DRUG — check against the chart
Right DOSE — calculate, then verify
Right ROUTE — never assume
Right TIME — and the right frequency
Check the label three times: taking it out, preparing it, returning it.
The three that get nurses struck off
Right DOCUMENTATION
Sign AFTER giving, never before
Right REASON
Why is this patient on this drug?
Right RESPONSE
Did it work? Did it harm?
Signing for a dose you did not give is falsifying
a record — a disciplinary matter, not an error.
Right to refuse — the patient has rights too
A competent adult may refuse any medicine, including one that is keeping them alive.
Find out WHY they are refusing. Side effects, cost, beliefs, or nobody ever explained it.
Explain, document the refusal and the reason, and inform the prescriber.
Hiding medicine in food without the patient's knowledge is covert administration and needs specific authority.
When you make an error — the order matters
1. ASSESS THE PATIENT FIRST. Observations, symptoms, the effect of what was given.
2. Tell the prescriber and the nurse in charge immediately.
3. Complete the incident form. Record facts in the notes — not the word 'error', not blame.
4. Never conceal it, and never try to correct it quietly with another drug.
The patient comes before the paperwork, and honesty is the only defensible position. Concealment ends careers.
